newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: FOCUS - OPEC trusts winter will mop up Iraqi oil.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - OPEC trusts winter will mop up Iraqi oil.

text.p: OPEC oil exporters who assembled in Vienna on Tuesday were banking on Western consumer demand for winter fuel to soak up any resumed Iraqi sales and prevent a big drop in petroleum prices.

Delegates said the Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries at talks that begin on Wednesday would see no need to adjust output quotas following progress at the United Nations towards finally easing the 1990 Gulf War ban on sales by Iraq.
"They did more than enough already", said Iraq's own chief delegate, Osama al-Hiti. He recalled that extra Iraqi oil was pencilled in under the quota system at talks in June.
In other significant comments, a Gulf source said OPEC linchpin Saudi Arabia believed oil demand is strong enough to absorb Iraqi sales -- if these materialise.
"The market is very healthy. Demand is strong. Stocks are low. And winter has just started," the source said, giving an insight into Saudi views ahead of Wednesday's OPEC talks.

The Saudis and Gulf allies Kuwait and the United Arab Emirates seemed ready to add their weight, probably decisive, behind the idea of simply extending OPEC's current quota pact through to the middle of 1997.

This accord, reached in June, wrote in an extra 800,000 barrels daily from Iraq. The Baghdad government said on Monday that it was ready to resume sales of oil for the first time since the Gulf War after agreeing to United Nations conditions under its "oil for food" plan.

Violations of OPEC's mandated quotas are said by Western monitors to have lifted actual production, even without any Iraqi sales, by as much as a million barrels daily above the agreed ceiling of 25.03 million.
But the Saudis and other key OPEC nations seem to feel that, vexing as this may be, the market can absorb more oil.

Snow greeted the ministers as they flew into Vienna on Tuesday. It was a reminder that oil companies are frantically trying to rebuild very low stocks of heating fuel ahead of what looks so far like being a harsh northern winter.
"Demand is whatever OPEC is producing", the Gulf source said. "We will definitely end this year with the lowest stocks in 20 years".

Benchmark Brent Blend crude dropped some 40 cents on Monday on news from New York that Iraq had accepted conditions for the delayed implementation of the U.N. accord to let it sell oil worth $2 billion to buy food and medicine.
But Brent stabilised on Tuesday above $22.50 per barrel, not too far off the recent post-Gulf War highs to which it was driven by the scramble to fill depleted stocks.
Independent analysts agreed that the market is unlikely to collapse, although they predict that Iraqi sales plus OPEC quota violations may mean some erosion of prices in 1997.
"The market is tight and it can take anything that is thrown at it right now", said Geoff Pyne, an energy economist with UBS Limited in London.
"But if Iraq returns soon it could be that prices will soften more quickly in the spring than we had expected".
With Iraq selling again, Pyne predicts an average 1997 price for the benchmark Brent Blend of North Sea crude at around $18.50 per barrel compared with $20 so far this year.

Allowing for inflation, a barrel of oil costing $18.50 is modestly better -- by about $3.50 in today's money -- than the price in 1973 when an Arab oil embargo on the West gave OPEC a chance to assert itself as a cartel.

But it compares with OPEC's own declared target of $21 for a basket of world crude oils -- equating to about $22 for Brent -- set as long ago as 1990, just before Iraq invaded fellow founder member Kuwait and provoked the U.N. ban on its oil.

Iran's oil minister, Gholamreza Aqazadeh, told reporters on Tuesday after a session of OPEC's own quota compliance committee that members who are alleged to be exceeding their quotas have mostly denied any infringement.
Just one member, Venezuela, is alone alleged to be in excess by 800,000 barrels, or as much as OPEC allocated Iraq.
